e.etymology: The feminine form of Karl, from a Germanic word for a free man that also gives Charles. The K spelling follows German and Scandinavian usage and is also common in Latin America.
From Old High German brun, 'brown', the name of medieval German and Italian saints, including the founder of the Carthusian order.
namesakes: Bruno Mars (pop singer)
Bruno Madrigal (the uncle in Disney's Encanto)
Bruno Tonioli (Dancing with the Stars judge)

assoc.t: We Don't Talk About Bruno, hit song from Encanto
Bruno Mars, pop singer

e.etymology: From the English surname, or a short form of Casey. As a first name it rose in the US in the 2000s alongside Chase, Cash and Cade.

assoc.t: case, the everyday word (court case, phone case)
Case IH, farm and construction equipment maker

e.etymology: From Mount Everest, the world's highest peak, named in 1865 for the British surveyor Sir George Everest. His surname may come from Evreux in Normandy.

assoc.t: Mount Everest, the world's highest mountain
Everest, the husky pup in PAW Patrol

e.etymology: The name of Saint Monica, the North African mother of Saint Augustine. Its meaning is uncertain, and its roots are probably Berber or Punic, not Latin.
namesakes: Monica Geller (character on Friends)
Monica Lewinsky (White House intern in the Clinton scandal)
Monica (R&B singer)

assoc.t: Monica Geller on the sitcom Friends
Monica Lewinsky, of the 1998 Clinton scandal
Monica, R&B singer of The Boy Is Mine

e.etymology: A Scandinavian elaboration of Karin, a short form of Katarina, long linked with Greek katharos, 'pure'. It is also a spelling of Carina, from Latin cara, 'dear'.
A modern name of uncertain origin. It is often linked to the biblical Hebrew Amariah, 'God has said', and it resembles Amari and Amara, but none of these links is documented.
The French form of Julia, the feminine of the Roman family name Julius, whose root is uncertain. It was a top-20 US girls' name around 1970.
namesakes: Julie Andrews (actress, The Sound of Music)
Julie Bowen (actress, Modern Family)
Julie Chen Moonves (TV host, Big Brother)

e.etymology: A short form of Calvin, Caleb, Callum and other Cal- names, now given on its own. Calvin is from a French surname meaning 'bald'; Caleb is Hebrew.
namesakes: Cal Ripken Jr. (Baseball Hall of Fame shortstop)

assoc.t: Cal, the University of California, Berkeley
short for California, as in SoCal and NorCal

e.etymology: From the English word promise, which comes from Latin promissum, 'something sent forth, a pledge'. It is one of the modern word names, like Journey and Destiny.
The Hebrew form of Hannah, from a root meaning 'grace' or 'favor'. In the Bible she is the mother of the prophet Samuel. In the US it is used mostly in Orthodox Jewish families.

assoc.t: chana, Hindi for chickpeas, as in chana masala

e.note: The Hebrew ch is a throaty h, not the ch of chair. Chana is also the Hindi word for chickpeas.

e.etymology: The Greek goddess of the hunt, wild animals and the moon, twin sister of Apollo. The origin of her name is uncertain.
namesakes: Artemis (Greek goddess of the hunt)
Artemis Fowl (boy genius of Eoin Colfer's novels)

assoc.t: Artemis, Greek goddess of the hunt and the moon
Artemis, NASA's program to return to the Moon
Artemis Fowl, boy genius of the fantasy novels

e.etymology: From Harlem, the Manhattan neighborhood at the center of Black American culture, which Dutch settlers named in 1658 after the city of Haarlem in the Netherlands.

assoc.t: Harlem, Manhattan neighborhood and Black cultural hub
Harlem Renaissance, 1920s Black arts movement
Harlem Globetrotters, exhibition basketball team
Harlem Shake, dance and 2013 viral video meme

e.etymology: A respelling of Leilani, from Hawaiian lei, 'garland of flowers', and lani, 'sky, heaven'.
From Hebrew Azar'el, 'God has helped'. In Islamic and some Jewish tradition Azrael is the angel of death, who separates souls from their bodies.

assoc.t: Azrael, angel of death in Islamic and Jewish lore
Azrael, Gargamel's cat in The Smurfs
Azrael, DC Comics vigilante in the Batman titles

e.note: Best known as the name of the angel of death.

e.etymology: As a girls' name, the medieval English feminine of John, from Old French Johanne; as a boys' name, the Catalan form of John. Both go back to Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
namesakes: Joan of Arc (French saint and military heroine)
Joan Rivers (comedian)
Joan Jett (rock musician)
e.note: US boys named Joan are mostly from Spanish-speaking families, where it is a male form of John said joh-AHN.

assoc.t: Joan of Arc, French heroine and saint

e.etymology: In Greek myth, the daughter of Demeter who was carried off by Hades and became queen of the underworld; her yearly return brings spring. The meaning of the name is uncertain.
namesakes: Persephone (Greek goddess of spring and queen of the underworld)

assoc.t: Persephone, Greek goddess and queen of the underworld

e.etymology: From the green gemstone, whose name comes through Old French esmeraude from Greek smaragdos. It is the English counterpart of the Spanish name Esmeralda.

assoc.t: emerald, green gemstone and May birthstone
Emerald, snack nuts brand

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins the popular Ky- opening to the -aire sound heard in Zaire. It has no meaning of its own.
A variant of Lauretta, the Italian pet form of Laura, from Latin laurus, 'laurel'. Among Catholics it also honors Our Lady of Loreto, a Marian shrine in Italy.
namesakes: Loretta Lynn (country music legend)
Loretta Young (classic Hollywood actress)
Loretta Lynch (US attorney general)

assoc.t: Loretta Lynn, country singer, the Coal Miner's Daughter

e.etymology: A spelling of Rain, the weather word, shaped by the surname Raine, which comes from Old French reine, 'queen', or from Germanic names in ragin, 'counsel'.
From the Southeast Asian country, whose name joins Malay with the Greek-style ending -sia. It came into use for American girls in the late 20th century, alongside Asia, India and Kenya.

assoc.t: Malaysia, Southeast Asian country

e.etymology: A variant of Eileen, the English form of Irish Eibhlin, which came from the Norman French name Aveline. The Ai- spelling is the usual one in Scotland.
namesakes: Aileen Wuornos (serial killer portrayed in the film Monster)

e.etymology: A Spanish-language form of the French name Arlette, popular in Mexico. Arlette is medieval French; it is often tied to Herleva, the mother of William the Conqueror, but its root is uncertain.
From the English word for rhythm or the closing notes of a musical phrase, which goes back to Latin cadere, 'to fall'. It rose quickly as a name in the early 2000s.
A pet form of Rocco and Rock, and a nickname for a tough man. Boxer Rocky Marciano, born Rocco, made it famous in the 1950s, and the Rocky films did so again from 1976.
namesakes: Rocky Balboa (boxer hero of the Rocky films)
Rocky Marciano (undefeated heavyweight champion)
ASAP Rocky (rapper)

assoc.t: Rocky Balboa, Sylvester Stallone's movie boxer
the Rocky Mountains, the Rockies
Rocky the Flying Squirrel of Rocky and Bullwinkle
The Rocky Horror Picture Show, cult musical film

e.etymology: Probably a respelling of Alia, from Arabic aliya, 'high, exalted', the root also behind Aaliyah. Some parents treat it as Leah with an added A.
The English form of Irish Brighid, 'exalted one', the name of a Celtic goddess and of Saint Brigid of Kildare, one of Ireland's patron saints.
namesakes: Bridget Jones (heroine of Bridget Jones's Diary)
Bridget Fonda (actress)
Bridget Moynahan (actress, Blue Bloods)

assoc.t: Bridget Jones, diary-writing heroine of books and films

e.etymology: The feminine of Theodore, from Greek theos, 'god', and doron, 'gift'. Two Byzantine empresses bore it. Dorothea uses the same two words in reverse order.
namesakes: Empress Theodora (wife of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins the word lake to the popular -lynn ending, on the pattern of Brooklynn and Oaklynn.
A Latinized form of Louise, the feminine of Louis, from the Germanic name Chlodovech, 'famous in battle'. It has been used in English since the 18th century.
namesakes: Louisa May Alcott (author of Little Women)

e.etymology: From Arabic hasan, 'good, handsome'. Hasan ibn Ali was the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad. The spelling Hassan also renders a separate Arabic name, Hassaan, 'doer of good'.
